description:
Dawn over Gangnam. A window on a high floor.

A man in a good suit stands alone in an unlit living room.
Beyond the glass, the city bleeds the blue of the hour before it wakes.

A phone on the table. A few missed calls. The man looks down at them for a moment.
Then he turns his eyes back to the window.

His face cannot be seen.

Who this man is — that part is yours to decide.

choices.text: Go back five years
choices.result_text:
Five years earlier.
Before any of it.

title: January 2026, Seoul
description:
Eyes open in the dark.

A room where you can touch the ceiling. Four-and-a-half square meters. The window faces the wall of the next building. A goshiwon — a micro-studio — in Sinchon. {name}'s room.

{name}. Thirty-three.
Yesterday, he made the last payment on six years of debt.

The confirmation message still glows on the thin desk. The date on the screen pulls up a scene he has spent years trying to bury.

choices.text: Close your eyes. Go back six years.
choices.result_text:
The winter light disappears behind his eyelids.
In its place: the cold floor of his father's entryway in Changwon.

title: The Gap
description:
Winter, age twenty-seven. The entryway of his father's home in Changwon.

Three unfamiliar pairs of dress shoes sit beside Dad's work boots. The living-room door is open by the width of a palm.

Cold vinyl seeps through {name}'s socks. A man's low voice carries from the other side.

"This isn't going to produce money you don't have."

choices.text: Put a hand against the door
choices.result_text:
{name} cannot make himself open it. He widens the gap by an inch.
The floor, the edge of the table, and the back of his father's head enter his view.

title: On His Knees
description:
Guarantee papers lie open on the table. The stamp mark is the only bright red in the room.

Dad is on his knees on the vinyl floor. Gray has begun to spread across the bowed back of his head. His hands rest awkwardly on his thighs.

"I'm sorry. I'll repay it."

The man across from him does not raise his voice. He checks the time on his phone and sighs.

"You said that already."

choices.text: Watch Dad open his mouth again
choices.result_text:
Dad's palms touch the floor.

"I'm sorry. I promise I'll repay it."

The same sentence is placed in the room one more time. The creditor turns a page.
Behind the door, {name} closes his fist until his nails cut into his palm.

title: Who I Was That Day
description:
No one knows {name} is behind the door.

There is room for one step between his father's knees and those guarantee papers. But twenty-seven-year-old {name} has no money to place there.

The doorknob is right in front of him.

choices.text: Rush in and pull Dad to his feet
choices.result_text:
{name} opens the door and takes hold of his father's elbows.

"Please. Get up."

Dad raises his head. That day, {name} looks him straight in the eye. He has no money to repay them, but he refuses to disappear.

choices.text: Clench your fist behind the door. You have no money to step in.
choices.result_text:
{name} stays behind the door.

When he opens his fist, half-moon marks cover his palm. Walking into the room would change nothing. There is nothing he can do.

The person {name} hates most that day is not anyone inside.

choices.text: Turn away. You cannot bear to watch.
choices.result_text:
{name} opens the front door without a sound and leaves.

He takes the stairs two at a time. Another apology carries from behind him. This time, he does not turn.

The harder he tries to erase that day, the sharper it becomes.

title: Ticket 147
description:
Yesterday. Six years later.

The display reads 146. {name} holds ticket 147 and the final repayment papers. Fluorescent lights hum in a perfectly even row.

He opens the transfer confirmation again. This is the end of it. The last payment of six years.

Balance: 500,000 won.

choices.text: Press down the corner of the papers and wait
choices.result_text:
The display sounds a short tone.

[Customer 147, please proceed to Window 4.]

{name} stands without managing to smooth the crease he has pressed into the papers.

title: The Last Payment
description:
The man behind the window checks the transfer against the papers twice. He stamps the release and slides it toward {name}.

"Payment confirmed. That settles it."

He is already looking at the next number. Aligning the papers in front of him, he adds without looking up:

"Tell your father you don't co-sign a loan for just anyone."

It is not advice. Just a sentence worn smooth from repetition.

choices.text: Bow your head and take the papers
choices.result_text:
"Okay."

It is a skill six years have taught him: swallow the sentence, take the paper, walk to the next door.

{name} folds the release twice and slips it inside his coat.

choices.text: "That was out of line."
choices.result_text:
The man finally looks up.

"The account is settled. Someone else is waiting."

There is no apology. Nothing changes. Still, {name} leaves one sentence behind in his own voice before he turns away.

choices.text: Smile, as if to say: just wait.
choices.result_text:
{name} raises the corners of his mouth.

"Sure. I'll tell him."

His reflection in the glass is not smiling. Someday, he thinks, this man will see what six years of repayment made.

title: Outside
description:
Winter rain falls outside. Water runs down the bus-shelter glass, catching the headlights from the road.

The ad panel changes: a bright living room suspended over Gangnam at night. [A city where your place is waiting.]

{name} opens the banking app.

Balance: 500,000 won.

Then the phone rings. DAD.

choices.text: Answer
choices.result_text:
The living room from six years ago overlaps with the window he just left.
{name} takes one breath and accepts the call.

title: A Call
description:
Winter rain taps against the bus-shelter roof. {name} presses Answer with a wet palm. The screen reads DAD.

"Hey, son. Where are you?"
"At the bus stop."

A television murmurs somewhere behind his father's voice. Dad always sends silence ahead of whatever he means to say.

"...You eat yet?"

He does not ask about work, money, or Seoul. Yet the whole of the last six years sits inside that one question: guilt, shame, everything neither of them can bring up first.

Before {name} answers, it feels as though his empty stomach has already given him away.

choices.text: "Yeah, I ate. Don't skip meals, Dad."
choices.result_text:
It is a lie. He has eaten nothing he could call dinner.

"Yeah, I ate. Don't skip meals, Dad."
On the other end, his breathing eases.
"Good... I'm sorry, son."
"Nothing to be sorry for."

As the call ends, a bus pulls in. {name} wipes the wet screen on his sleeve and climbs aboard. Two lies, each meant to put the other man at ease, follow him home.

choices.text: "I'm busy. I'll call you back." Click.
choices.result_text:
"I'm busy. I'll call you later."

{name} speaks over him and ends the call. Longer calls leave room for silence, and silence makes space for questions neither of them can answer. He wants none of it.

The bus-shelter light and his face overlap in the dead screen. Just before Dad says "Okay," he stops breathing for half a beat. When the bus arrives, {name} climbs aboard instead of answering that pause.

title: The Notebook
description:
Back at the goshiwon, {name} hangs up his wet coat and opens a worn notebook.

The Gangnam apartment his father spent a lifetime saving for. The one the fraud took. Dad has never spoken of it since.

The doctor said not to overwork, but gave no number for the time left. So {name} sets the deadline himself.

Five years. Three billion won.

The pen stops before the numbers. What this money is for — that sentence has to be his.

choices.text: I will give my father a home again.
choices.result_text:
{name} writes the first line.

I will give my father a home again.

Under it: three billion won, five years. There is no plan yet. But the reason for earning it is finally clear.

choices.text: I will stand in my own name inside the world that broke us.
choices.result_text:
{name} writes the first line.

I will stand in my own name inside the world that broke us.

Under it: three billion won, five years. He wants his name at the door, not at the bottom of somebody else's papers.

choices.text: I will never kneel before money again.
choices.result_text:
{name} writes the first line.

I will never kneel before money again.

Under it: three billion won, five years. The cold of the vinyl floor beyond that door still lingers beneath his feet.

title: First Meal
description:
Out of the goshiwon, into the convenience store.

You think about the bank balance. 500,000 won.
Next month's goshiwon rent is 650,000 won. Already in the red.

Standing in front of the shelves, {name} does the math.
One triangle kimbap: 1,200 won. Should you even buy it?

Less than ten thousand won to spend each day. Holding the triangle kimbap, {name} looks from the register to the exit.

choices.text: Buy a triangle kimbap (-1,200 won)
choices.result_text:
You grab a tuna-mayo and pay.
The balance printed at the bottom of the receipt is 1,200 won lower.

choices.text: Skip it. Save every won.
choices.result_text:
You walk out empty-handed.
Your stomach growls. The convenience-store light recedes behind you.

title: Can't Wait Any Longer
description:
Two weeks in.

The balance is already shrinking. Income: 0 won.
At this rate you won't last a month.

Another wedding announcement in the old high school group chat.
{name} types 'Congrats' and flips the phone face-down.

A moment later, {name} picks it up again. His finger stops over the job app on the home screen.

choices.text: Open a job app. Survival comes first.
choices.result_text:
Convenience store. Delivery. Café. Office temp...
{name} rests his finger over the first Apply button.

title: Half a Year Gone
description:
Six calendar pages had turned. On the day {name} first entered this room, a suitcase wheel caught on the threshold and there was only five hundred thousand won in the bank. The damp wallpaper smell from that day still rose whenever it rained.

He pushed the receipts and notes on the desk to one side. Some numbers had changed. Other things had not. Was this progress, or had he merely learned how to endure?

Beyond the small window, Seoul's lights moved as quickly as they had on the first night. The city did not slow down for someone just because he had survived half a year inside it.

choices.text: I held on well. Let's keep going.
choices.result_text:
"You held on." Saying it aloud felt a little embarrassing.

Before the account balance, {name} remembered the mornings he had not missed and the nights he had managed to stand up again. He folded the old calendar page and put it in the drawer.

He was still here. For once, that fact did not feel small.

choices.text: Still not enough. I need to move faster.
choices.result_text:
{name} reopened the planner and filled every blank with a task. The harder he wrote, the deeper the pen pressed into the paper.

When you speed up, the scenery is the first thing to blur. He knew that and moved his alarm an hour earlier anyway.

Long after the light went out, the boxes of the new schedule remained behind his eyelids.

choices.text: Just rest. Today, at least, I won't think about anything.
choices.result_text:
{name} turned the phone face-down and slept for half the day. When he woke, the angle of the light in the room had changed.

At first his chest tightened with the sense of time thrown away. After a hot shower, his shoulders finally dropped.

That night he did not snooze the alarm. The hours spent resting had not vanished after all.

title: A Year Gone
description:
Twelve months.

{name}.

This time last year you unpacked your bags in this room for the first time.
Back then you didn't even know how big Seoul was.

And now?

If you're still in a goshiwon, something feels like it's going wrong;
if you're living in an apartment, you got lucky, or you really did well.
Wherever you are, the fact remains: you survived a year.

How hard it is to hang on in Seoul,
only someone who has hung on truly knows.

choices.text: Just making it this far means something
choices.result_text:
I decided not to compare.
{name} is moving at {name}'s own pace.
Even if that pace looks slow, it isn't a stop.

choices.text: A year passed and I'm still here? Time to burn bright.
choices.result_text:
I lit the flame.
I just hope this energy lasts.
{name} already knows: restlessness and resolve are different things.

title: A Rainy Night
description:
At eleven, rain tapped a dense rhythm against the goshiwon's small window. The canned coffee from the hallway machine held only a palmful of warmth. Wet slippers left thin marks across the floor.

{name} sat on the edge of the bed and turned off the fluorescent light. Only the rain and a low cough from the next room remained. Had he lived this day properly? Did he still remember why he had come to Seoul?

The can lost its warmth first. The questions stayed, and the rain answered neither one.

choices.text: Yeah, one step at a time. I won't give up.
choices.result_text:
{name} swallowed a mouthful of lukewarm coffee. The bitterness lingered on his tongue.

He wrote one thing at the top of tomorrow's list. Not a grand resolution, just something he could do the moment he got up.

The rain went on, but the room now held one small sequence of events. That was enough to begin again.

choices.text: I'm worn out. I'll just rest today.
choices.result_text:
{name} switched off the alarm and pulled the blanket to his chin. The unfinished tasks knocked around in his head for a while, until the rain covered them one by one.

For the first time in weeks, he slept without waking in the middle. The window was still gray in the morning, and the work was still there.

But when he sat up, he felt a little more present inside his own body than he had the night before.

title: News from a Friend
description:
A KakaoTalk alert appeared. A friend from high school.

'I got into a major company lol'

{name}'s thumb stopped above Send halfway through a congratulatory message. In the profile photo, his friend wore an employee badge; a clean glass office tower rose behind him. They had come to Seoul in the same year. One of them already belonged inside a company people knew. {name} was still waiting to hear back from applications.

The harder he tried not to compare them, the sharper their two positions became. When the screen went dark, the employee badge disappeared and left only his own reflection.

choices.text: I'm genuinely happy for them. I have my own path.
choices.result_text:
"Seriously, congratulations. You worked for it."

A grinning sticker came back almost at once. Pride for his friend and the ache in his own stomach occupied the same place. Neither feeling had to make the other one false.

{name} left the conversation near the top of his inbox. Even after he closed the app, the congratulations remained sincere.

choices.text: It lit a fire under me. I should work harder.
choices.result_text:
{name} sent a quick congratulations and opened the laptop. Every job posting suddenly looked close to its deadline.

He revised one more line, submitted one more application, then another whenever the employee badge returned to mind. By dawn his eyes burned and three confirmation emails sat in the inbox.

A spark could drive a person forward or burn through him. Tonight, he could not yet tell which this was.

choices.text: Close the SNS app. Now is the time to focus on what's mine.
choices.result_text:
After replying, {name} closed the social app and silenced its alerts. On the quiet screen he wrote only what he could do now: one resume, one meal, a thirty-minute walk.

His friend's pace had not disappeared. It simply no longer occupied the desk tonight.

{name} returned to his own time. It was smaller than the life on the profile page, but it was a size he could hold.

title: First Paycheck
description:
Near the end of the shift, a short vibration announced a bank deposit.

[DEPOSIT] SALARY

{name} looked at the amount, opened the app, and checked it again. After tax, rent, and food, the money would not remain for long. But it was not an allowance or something borrowed. The hours spent showing up on time and holding himself together among strangers had become a number beneath his own name.

When he turned off the screen, the vibration seemed to remain in his palm. The first paycheck registered as weight before it registered as money.

choices.text: Buy my parents something with my first paycheck
choices.result_text:
{name} sent his parents a small gift card. Choosing the amount took longer than checking the paycheck had.

The reply came soon: 'You should save your money.' Their happiness showed through the warning anyway.

He read the message several times without clearing it. Only after some of that first paycheck left the account did the rest of it feel as though it truly belonged to him.

choices.text: Save it all. The future comes before feelings.
choices.result_text:
{name} moved the whole paycheck into savings. The deposit notification was replaced almost immediately by a transfer receipt, and the feeling folded itself beneath another line of numbers.

He listed next month's fixed expenses and calculated what remained. There was less room to celebrate than there was money to protect.

The balance did not grow while the app was closed, but for the first time he had given every won a place to stand.

choices.text: Buy a small gift for myself, who worked so hard
choices.result_text:
After a long hesitation, {name} bought a new pair of sneakers. They were not expensive, yet pressing Pay felt like asking himself for permission.

The box smelled of rubber and new fabric. The next morning the heels rubbed raw, and he kept looking down at them on the way to work.

The first thing he bought with wages he had earned was not perfect. That made it feel more likely to stay in his memory.

title: Working Late
description:
At ten, the cleaning cart rolled past once and left {name} alone in the office. One row of fluorescent lights hummed overhead. His dry eyes stung at the edge of the monitor.

Anything unfinished tonight would move into tomorrow. Tomorrow's work was already waiting, which meant one delayed day could follow him into the next night. He rested a hand over Save and looked outside. Only a few windows remained lit in the building opposite.

Somewhere in Seoul, other people had already ended their day. His was the only one in the room that had not been allowed to leave.

choices.text: Finish it and go. Home's just a goshiwon anyway.
choices.result_text:
At 11:30, the last file went through. Only when the delivery receipt appeared did {name} notice the pain in his shoulders.

He fell asleep with his head against the bus window and woke two stops beyond home, then walked back through the cold.

The deadline was gone and tomorrow had become a little lighter. Today's exhaustion remained exactly where it had settled in his body.

choices.text: Just clock out today. Tomorrow's work is for tomorrow.
choices.result_text:
{name} saved the file and shut down the computer. The sign-off tone sounded enormous in the empty office. Tomorrow's disapproval seemed to be waiting beyond the door, but he left anyway.

On the way home, convenience-store fish-cake broth burned his tongue. He wrapped both hands around the paper cup until feeling returned to his fingers.

There was unfinished work behind him, and one evening he had managed not to surrender with it.

choices.text: Grab one more coffee and push through
choices.result_text:
{name} bought one more vending-machine coffee. The sweetness numbed his tongue and put his hands back in motion.

At one in the morning he closed the file. His exhausted face floated in the office glass. Relief arrived together with the fatigue already waiting for tomorrow.

The elevator numbers descended slowly. He still could not tell which part of this was making him stronger, and which part was simply wearing him away.

title: Saturday Morning
description:
Saturday, nine in the morning. No alarm had gone off, but {name} woke at the weekday hour anyway. His body tensed as though reaching for a subway strap. Only the refrigerator motor turned in the room.

He did not have to do anything today. Lying still, however, felt as if somebody else were taking his share of time first. His eyes followed an old stain across the ceiling.

Even on a day off, the sensation of falling behind did not rest. He could not yet decide whether the guilt was discipline or fear.

choices.text: Go to a cafe and study. Time is precious.
choices.result_text:
{name} carried the laptop and books to a cafe and stayed at a window seat for four hours. As the highlighted lines multiplied, so did the relief of having used the morning correctly.

By the time he stepped outside, the sun had already dropped. He had learned something, certainly. He had not rested.

He adjusted the heavy bag on his shoulder. One square of the weekend closed neatly inside the plan.

choices.text: Just rest. I'll give this one day to myself.
choices.result_text:
{name} put the phone out of reach and lay down again. After a late lunch, he walked the neighborhood without a destination. For once he noticed the plants outside the laundromat and paw prints dried into an alley.

By evening there was nothing he could call an achievement. His breathing had deepened.

Next week had not become easier, but the body that would have to enter it had begun to return.

choices.text: Go out to meet a friend
choices.result_text:
{name} met a friend and talked about nothing important: bad bosses, expensive food, an old homeroom teacher. He laughed hard enough to swallow water wrong and cough for a full minute.

On the subway home, his face muscles felt faintly sore. Not once had they discussed the goal or the balance in his account.

Seeing people in Seoul cost time and money. Still, the silence on the way back felt different from the usual kind.

title: The Person Next Door
description:
After several months in the goshiwon, {name} still remembered only the lower half of the neighbor's face. Whenever they met in the hall, one flattened against the wall and the other studied his slippers. They knew only how quickly the other's door closed.

At night, alarms, coughs, and the tear of ramyeon lids traveled through the wall. They were the sounds of people who had come to this narrow place for reasons of their own, people who had learned that not asking was a form of courtesy.

They met again by the shared sink. Between bursts of running water, {name} wondered if he could be the first to speak.

choices.text: Offer a single 'Hello'
choices.result_text:
"Hello."

The neighbor looked surprised, then dipped his head. "Oh. Hi." That was the entire conversation. They went back to their separate rooms.

When they met again that night, both nodded before either body moved aside. The walls had not shifted, yet the hall seemed a little less narrow. They still did not know each other's names. The greeting remained.

choices.text: Just pass by. It's easier not to get involved.
choices.result_text:
{name} shook the water from his hands and passed with his eyes down. The neighbor moved toward the wall at the same instant. Their shoulders did not touch.

{name}'s lock clicked, and the next door answered almost at once. If you never got involved, there were fewer ways to be hurt.

He was learning the convenience of that rule. Still, whenever the cough came through the wall, he briefly saw the face he had chosen not to acknowledge.

title: Payday
description:
On the morning of the twenty-fifth, {name} opened the banking app as the commuter train crossed the river. His arm swayed on the overhead strap, and the screen moved with it. The number at the top of the account had changed. Payday.

Calculation came before pleasure: rent, transit, phone bill, the next card payment. A month of labor shrank within a few lines of subtraction. Still, the early alarms, packed transfers, and words swallowed at work all existed inside that number.

The train entered a tunnel and his face appeared over the account. Payday came every month. He was not yet numb to it.

choices.text: Save it all. Now is the time to scrimp.
choices.result_text:
As soon as {name} moved the money into savings, the deposit alert became a transfer receipt. The paycheck had not stayed where it arrived for long.

He closed the shopping cart he had been keeping and left only next month's fixed expenses. Satisfaction at having resisted arrived beside the thought of living another month exactly this way.

He checked the balance once more. Unspent money made no noise, but it remained on his side.

choices.text: Buy a small gift for myself, who worked so hard
choices.result_text:
{name} bought new sneakers after work. Even after walking in front of the store mirror, he hesitated until the moment of payment.

The next day they rubbed one heel raw. Still, as he tied the new laces, the month no longer seemed to have vanished entirely into fixed expenses.

It was not an expensive gift. It was a piece of the paycheck that stayed beneath his feet, where he could see it every day.

choices.text: Think about how to grow this money
choices.result_text:
{name} listed income and expenses line by line. The money he imagined remained and the money that truly remained were not the same.

Once the figures had names, he could see what was available to invest. He could also see the line beyond which one mistake would reach next month's rent.

He underlined that boundary. Growing money began with knowing which money must not be touched.

title: Thinking of Home
description:
On the evening before the holiday rush, the news showed long lines at the express bus terminal. People hurried beneath the departure board carrying gift boxes. {name} opened the booking app and stared at the seats.

At home, the same questions would be waiting on the table. Do you have a job? Have you saved anything? How is Seoul? He knew they asked because they worried. He still had no sentence ready for them.

Seoul was suffocating, and home felt too heavy to return to. As more buses turned red with SOLD OUT, the smell of his mother's soup came back with impossible clarity.

choices.text: Go down anyway. I miss my parents.
choices.result_text:
{name} caught a canceled seat and went home. Opening the door released the smell of sesame oil and the sound of the television. The table held too many dishes for three people.

The questions arrived exactly as expected. He answered that what he did not know, he did not know; what had not happened yet, had not happened yet. Nothing terrible followed.

On the bus back to Seoul, the bag of side dishes was heavy. His chest was somehow lighter than it had been on the way down.

choices.text: Stay in Seoul this year. This is the right call.
choices.result_text:
{name} did not buy a ticket. He only called. "Work came up this year." His mother went quiet, then told him not to skip meals. Television laughter traveled through the phone.

On the holiday morning, the goshiwon hallway was quieter than usual. Most of the delivery apps still read NOT OPEN.

{name} poured hot water into instant soup. He had thought staying would be the easier choice. The smell of the empty corridor lasted longer than he expected.

title: The First Three Million Won
description:
{name} opened the banking app and stopped at the balance. It had crossed three million won. This was the account that held only five hundred thousand when he came to Seoul.

There was no grand success in the transaction history: wages, transit, convenience-store meals, rent. The small differences left after eating, sleeping, working, and closing things he wanted to buy had accumulated one line at a time.

Gangnam seemed almost no closer. The starting balance, however, had finally been pushed below the visible part of the screen. For the first time, {name} could see that money protected was also distance traveled.

choices.text: Protect this money and grow it further
choices.result_text:
{name} renamed the savings account DO NOT TOUCH. They were only words, but perhaps they would make his finger pause before every transfer.

The idea that preservation came before growth was not glamorous. Yet the path from five hundred thousand won to here had been made of small refusals, not one brilliant move.

He closed the app. For the first time, he felt less like someone earning money and more like someone capable of keeping it.

choices.text: It's time to move more aggressively
choices.result_text:
The fact that one number had been built made a larger number easy to imagine. {name} opened the investment app and returned to the assets he had only watched before.

Once he entered an order amount, three million won looked suddenly thin. The possible loss expanded with it. His finger remained closer to Confirm than Cancel.

The first real bet delivered a sensation before it delivered any return: the time he had saved was now capable of moving against him.

choices.text: Record this moment
choices.result_text:
{name} wrote down the date and balance, then took a screenshot. In the photo roll it looked like an ordinary banking screen.

Beneath it he added: 'Started with 500,000 won.' He could not know whether this amount would someday look tiny or remain the largest moment of all.

He closed the note. The goal was still far away, but one piece of evidence now proved that he had begun.

title: A Year and a Half
description:
Eighteen months.

Seoul isn't strange to you anymore.
The commute, the convenience store you frequent, the diner where you have lunch.
It's all familiar now.

But you're not sure being familiar is a good thing.
Are the things {name} wants still here?
Or is this just becoming the way you live?

You were browsing job listings, then closed the window.

choices.text: Now's the time. Prepare to switch jobs.
choices.result_text:
You pulled out your resume again.
You organized what you'd learned at your current job.
Even if it feels like you're not ready, the ones who move are the ones who catch the chance.

choices.text: Hold on a bit longer. Build more where I am.
choices.result_text:
Job-hopping later. For now you'll learn more here.
This is a time that needs depth more than haste.
{name} held the position again today.

choices.text: Decide not to think about it now. Just live today.
choices.result_text:
You closed the window and ate.
Some things just don't have an answer right now.
{name} is slowly learning to accept that.

title: Two Years
description:
Twenty-four months.

{name} has become a Seoulite.
Subway transfers, real estate apps, eating lunch in eight minutes flat.

You met your hometown friends for the first time in a while,
And they said your speech had changed a little.
That a Seoul accent had crept in.

Strangely, that made you a little wistful.
And at the same time, it felt like you'd become something.

Two years have passed.

choices.text: Resolve to put down deeper roots in Seoul
choices.result_text:
This became {name}'s city.
Someday you'll build something in this city.
That conviction took root, just a little.

choices.text: The changing me feels strange. Take a quick trip home.
choices.result_text:
You took the train down.
Eating the meal Mom made, you returned to childhood for a moment.
Heading back up to Seoul, {name} felt a little tougher.

title: Three Years
description:
Three years in Seoul. Thirty-six years old.

Wedding links, housewarming photos, and airport departures took turns appearing in the group chat. People who had worn the same school uniform now answered to different addresses and titles. Each time {name} pressed Congratulations, his own three years appeared beside theirs.

Gangnam was still far away. The numbers said it was closer than before; the calendar said he had already spent three years. Yet imagining himself folding up the goal made it harder to breathe.

{name} watched the chat go dark. What kept him here was less certainty than an inability to let go.

choices.text: My path is the right one. Different pace is fine.
choices.result_text:
{name} looked through the wedding and housewarming photos again and left congratulations. Then he opened his own ledger. Erasing other people's milestones would not create a road of his own.

He wrote the balance from three years ago beside today's. The start and speed were different. Movement was still visible.

He did not yet know whether the direction was right. He chose only to set the next step by his own record rather than someone else's clock.

choices.text: I have to move faster. Three years is long enough.
choices.result_text:
{name} marked the two years remaining and cut the plan into smaller pieces. Monthly goals became weekly goals; weekly goals became tonight's tasks.

This time, impatience seemed to have a direction. He postponed several plans and moved the alarm earlier.

As the desk calendar grew denser, other things were pushed off its edge. The gear went up. The view outside began to blur.

choices.text: Do everything I can right where I am
choices.result_text:
Instead of another grand plan, {name} wrote down three things for today: work, exercise, one hour of study. When each was done, he crossed it out.

The goal remained three billion won, but the only things within reach were these three boxes. Their smallness felt comforting rather than pathetic.

He closed the list before bed. Tomorrow would arrive in the same modest size. He chose to live that day properly too.

title: Four Years
description:
Year four. Thirty-seven. By now {name}'s body knew which subway stairs were fastest and which alley stayed least slippery in the rain. Whether he had escaped the goshiwon or still lived there, Seoul was no longer a strange city. It had become a set of habits.

These days he asked less often whether the road was right and more often whether the speed was enough. His assets had grown. Gangnam was closer than two years ago. The time remaining had shrunk even faster.

In the late train window, {name} studied his reflection. As he had grown used to the city, the old urgency had grown used to living in his face.

choices.text: Pick up the pace. Move more aggressively.
choices.result_text:
{name} erased every block marked margin and replaced it with growth or return. He answered opportunities he had postponed and chose greater volatility over familiar methods.

The decision brought relief, but his jaw remained tight. Forward motion and the sense of being chased could feel almost identical.

He left no time to test the difference. The final night of year four ran directly into the first appointment of year five.

choices.text: Stabilizing where I am comes first
choices.result_text:
{name} first listed the things beginning to shake: sleep, meals, debt, the calls he had put off too long. Before pushing the number higher, he would repair the floor beneath it.

For several days he slept earlier, reorganized automatic payments, and checked in with one person. Nothing produced a visible return. The pressure on his chest in the morning eased a little.

A foundation offered no scene worth boasting about. It would be proven later only by the days that did not collapse.

title: Thirty-Five
description:
Thirty-five.

{name} knows the weight this age carries in Korean society.
Marriage, owning a home, settling into a career.
People around you ask. Where do you live? Married yet?

{name}'s answer is still being prepared.
Gangnam is the goal. You're not there yet.

But the saying that opportunities shrink after thirty-five,
{name} has decided not to believe it.

There's still time.

choices.text: This is the most important turning point of my life. Go all in.
choices.result_text:
The skills have stacked up now. The timing is there too.
{name} read thirty-five not as 'not yet' but as 'now.'
There's no age limit on taking a chance.

choices.text: Stay unshaken. Protect my foundation.
choices.result_text:
Whatever anyone says, {name} has {name}'s own pace.
Not collapsing comes first.
From a solid foundation, aim for Gangnam.

title: The Final Half Year
description:
Thirty-eight was six months away. Twenty-four squares remained on the calendar.

A pay stub lay on the desk; the bank balance and portfolio glowed on the phone. {name} moved between the three, calculating the remaining distance to Gangnam again. The figures were familiar. His fingertips felt colder than before.

Five years had once sounded long. Now a single choice could change the shape of the weeks that remained. Dawn moved across the glass of the buildings outside.

One question weighed more than whether the goal was possible: what kind of person would pass through these final six months?

choices.text: Pour everything into the six months that remain
choices.result_text:
{name} cleared everything from the desk except the plan. Regret could wait until the end. Now was the time to put down every card that remained.

His hand shook as he entered the order, but he pressed Confirm. His heart ran fast. The room was unnaturally quiet.

He circled the final date on the calendar. Every blank square between here and there now faced in the same direction.

choices.text: Don't push it. What I've done so far is enough
choices.result_text:
{name} closed the apps and put the calculator in the drawer. This time he did not push away the thought that Gangnam might not be everything as if it were only an excuse.

He counted what remained: his body, the people around him, the things he had learned, the places that might still take him back. Not everything of value lived inside the number.

Cold air entered through the window. The goal had not vanished. For the first time, it looked smaller than he was.

choices.text: There's still a way. Run the numbers again
choices.result_text:
{name} opened a new sheet and divided the remaining twenty-four weeks into cells: income, fixed costs, tolerable loss. The numbers offered neither hope nor despair. They left only a cold range of possibility.

He marked the interval that remained unchanged after three calculations. The road was narrow, not fully closed.

By dawn, the limit he had to protect looked clearer on the screen than the chance he wanted to chase.

description_if_known.final_year_resolve:
Thirty-eight was six months away. Twenty-four squares remained on the calendar.

A pay stub lay on the desk; the bank balance and portfolio glowed on the phone. {name} moved between the three, calculating the remaining distance to Gangnam again. The figures were familiar. His fingertips felt colder than before.

A sentence from last year's reckoning returned: whatever the number, this trajectory was his. Dawn moved across the glass of the buildings outside.

One question weighed more than whether the goal was possible. Could he carry that sentence through the final six months without losing the person who had said it?
description_if_known.final_year_realistic:
Thirty-eight was six months away. Twenty-four squares remained on the calendar.

A pay stub lay on the desk; the bank balance and portfolio glowed on the phone. {name} moved between the three, calculating the remaining distance to Gangnam again. The figures were familiar. His fingertips felt colder than before.

Last year he had adjusted the plan and chosen to live the ending with his eyes open. This calculation was the last page of that decision.

The figures remained cold beneath the dawn light. Could he pass through these final six months without looking away from what they said?
description_if_known.final_year_open:
Thirty-eight was six months away. Twenty-four squares remained on the calendar.

A pay stub lay on the desk; the bank balance and portfolio glowed on the phone. {name} moved between the three, calculating the remaining distance to Gangnam again. The figures were familiar. His fingertips felt colder than before.

Last year he had closed the calculator and said he would know only at the end. The end now waited twenty-four squares away.

Dawn moved across the glass of the buildings outside. The final six months approached at the same speed even for someone who had postponed the answer.
description_if_known.accepted_current_path:
Thirty-eight was six months away. Twenty-four squares remained on the calendar.

A pay stub lay on the desk; the bank balance and portfolio glowed on the phone. {name} moved between the three, calculating the remaining distance to Gangnam again. The figures were familiar. His fingertips felt colder than before.

One night, he had chosen to accept the path he was on. Acceptance was not surrender. It was how he kept from living the time that remained as somebody else's failure.

One question now weighed more than whether Gangnam was possible: could he keep that choice his own for six more months?
description_if_known.final_push_decided:
Thirty-eight was six months away. Twenty-four squares remained on the calendar.

A pay stub lay on the desk; the bank balance and portfolio glowed on the phone. {name} moved between the three, calculating the remaining distance to Gangnam again. The figures were familiar. His fingertips felt colder than before.

One night, he had committed to a final push. Back then it was a sentence. Now it had become twenty-four actual weeks.

Dawn moved across the glass of the buildings outside. The spreadsheet still had no cell for the person who would remain when that commitment came due.

title: First Paycheck
description:
Near the end of the shift, a short vibration announced a bank deposit.

[DEPOSIT] SALARY

{name} looked at the amount, opened the app, and checked it again. After tax, rent, and food, the money would not remain for long. But it was not an allowance or something borrowed. The hours spent showing up on time and holding himself together among strangers had become a number beneath his own name.

When he turned off the screen, the vibration seemed to remain in his palm. The first paycheck registered as weight before it registered as money.

choices.text: Buy Mother something with my first paycheck
choices.result_text:
{name} sent Mother a small gift card. Choosing the amount took longer than checking the paycheck had.

Her reply came soon: 'Save your money. Your father would have loved to see this.'

Happiness and an empty place shared the same sentence. {name} read the message several times without clearing it.

choices.text: Save it all. The future comes before feelings.
choices.result_text:
{name} moved the whole paycheck into savings. The deposit notification was replaced almost immediately by a transfer receipt, and the feeling folded itself beneath another line of numbers.

He listed next month's fixed expenses and calculated what remained. There was less room to celebrate than there was money to protect.

The balance did not grow while the app was closed, but for the first time he had given every won a place to stand.

choices.text: Buy a small gift for myself, who worked so hard
choices.result_text:
After a long hesitation, {name} bought a new pair of sneakers. They were not expensive, yet pressing Pay felt like asking himself for permission.

The box smelled of rubber and new fabric. The next morning the heels rubbed raw, and he kept looking down at them on the way to work.

The first thing he bought with wages he had earned was not perfect. That made it feel more likely to stay in his memory.

title: Thinking of Home
description:
On the evening before the holiday rush, the news showed long lines at the express bus terminal. People hurried beneath the departure board carrying gift boxes. {name} opened the booking app and stared at the seats.

At home, a table Mother had prepared alone would be waiting, along with the pauses where neither of them knew how to begin talking about Father. {name} still had no ready answer for how life in Seoul was going.

Seoul was suffocating, and home felt too heavy to return to. As more buses turned red with SOLD OUT, the smell of Mother's soup came back with impossible clarity.

choices.text: Go down anyway. I don't want Mother to be alone.
choices.result_text:
{name} caught a canceled seat and went home. Opening the door released the smell of sesame oil and the sound of the television. The table held too many dishes for the people eating.

Mother asked about Seoul, and both of them paused whenever Father's name surfaced. {name} answered that what he did not know, he did not know; what had not happened yet, had not happened yet.

On the bus back to Seoul, the bag of side dishes was heavy. His chest was somehow lighter than it had been on the way down.

choices.text: Stay in Seoul this year. This is the right call.
choices.result_text:
{name} did not buy a ticket. He only called. "Work came up this year." His mother went quiet, then told him not to skip meals. Television laughter traveled through the phone.

On the holiday morning, the goshiwon hallway was quieter than usual. Most of the delivery apps still read NOT OPEN.

{name} poured hot water into instant soup. He had thought staying would be the easier choice. The smell of the empty corridor lasted longer than he expected.
